opus-5.5.text:
I think it's less that we'll need a brand-new category of problems and more that the Erdős problems are going to stop being the frontier fairly quickly, and that changes what we measure.

The Erdős problems have been a wonderful testbed. There are hundreds of them, they're stated cleanly, many are approachable without a huge amount of specialized machinery, and they span a range of difficulty, from things that turned out to have been essentially solved in the literature already to things that are genuinely deep and open. That makes them a good proving ground for whether a model can do something mathematically real rather than just recall textbook results.

But a lot of what's been happening is that models are finding the easier end of that distribution: problems where the right lemma already exists somewhere, or where a careful, patient argument gets you there. That's valuable, but it isn't the same as the kind of progress mathematicians care most about, which is developing new ideas, new frameworks, and new ways of seeing a whole area.

So the next step isn't so much a different category as a different mode of working. Instead of "here's an isolated problem, go solve it," it looks more like "here's a research program, help push it forward": generating conjectures, figuring out which intermediate statements are worth proving, connecting fields that don't usually talk to each other. That's harder to evaluate, because there's no clean answer key, and you need working mathematicians in the loop to judge whether something is actually interesting and not just technically correct.

I also think verification becomes more important as the problems get harder. When a model produces a long, novel argument, you want either a formal proof or very careful expert review, so I expect tighter integration with formal tools and with the mathematical community.

So, short answer: the Erdős problems will keep being useful for a while, but the real milestone isn't clearing the list. It's when these systems become genuine collaborators on open-ended research, and that's what we should be designing the next generation of challenges around.

r001.rationale: The response calls some Erdős problems “genuinely deep and open,” but does not judge the hardest problems to be far beyond the reach of current mathematical methods.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the answer is yes and no at the same time, and I want to be careful about why. The Erdős problems have been incredibly useful as a testbed precisely because they're a huge, heterogeneous collection. There are hundreds of them, they're crisply stated, and a lot of them have been sitting there for decades. That makes them a nice honest benchmark: you can't really overfit to a problem nobody has solved. So in that sense I don't think we've exhausted them. Plenty of the open ones still require genuinely new ideas, not just search or clever combination of known lemmas.

But if you look at the ones that have actually fallen recently, there's a pattern. A lot of them turned out to be either forgotten results living in some obscure paper, or problems where the right tool existed and nobody with that tool had looked at that problem. That's real progress, and it's useful, but it's a different kind of contribution than inventing a new technique. The model is acting a bit like an unusually well-read collaborator who connects the literature.

So the thing I actually care about is whether the next category of problems forces the model to build something, rather than find something. Open problems where the obstruction is conceptual, where you need a new object or a new framework, not just a search. Those exist among Erdős's questions too, but they're mixed in with the ones that were low-hanging in retrospect. I'd like benchmarks that separate those two cases more cleanly, because right now a solved Erdős problem can mean very different things.

And honestly, the most interesting version isn't a curated list at all. It's a mathematician working on their own research question, something nobody has written down as a numbered problem, and the model being useful in that setting. That's harder to measure, but it's closer to what we actually want.

r001.rationale: The candidate says some open Erdős problems require genuinely new ideas, but does not judge the hardest ones to be far beyond the reach of current mathematical methods.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we necessarily need a new category of problems. The Erdős problems already give us a pretty broad range of challenges. Some might yield to a clever application of existing techniques, while others might require genuinely new ideas. And figuring out which is which is itself part of the work.

I think the more useful question is whether we can make progress on problems where we don’t already know what the path to a solution looks like. Can we explore examples, formulate a useful intermediate conjecture, and change direction when an approach fails? You can study all of that within existing mathematics, including the Erdős problems.

r001.rationale: The response says some Erdős problems may yield to existing techniques and others may need new ideas, but it does not judge the hardest problems to be far beyond current mathematical methods.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t think we necessarily need a new category of problems. The Erdős problems already span a pretty wide range, from questions where you can try lots of concrete examples to ones that seem to require a genuinely new idea. What we need is progress in the ability to explore those questions, recognize useful structure, and turn that into a rigorous proof. Working on other kinds of problems could help develop those abilities, but I wouldn’t say that’s a prerequisite.
